plan: Sell all leveraged ETFs (SOXL, SPAL) to zero.

conservative.read: This conservative approach aims for lower monthly gains (~1.5%) by significantly reducing leverage and concentrating on income and broad market exposure. The primary risk is missing out on potential upside from strong tech rallies, with a focus on minimizing drawdowns.

plan: Trim leveraged ETFs (SOXL to 3%, SPAL to 2%) to reduce risk.
Trim SPY to 25% to lower concentration and increase cash buffer.
Buy Netflix (NFLX) at 4% as a new high-potential addition.
Buy Microsoft (MSFT) at 8% to add a strong tech name.

balanced.read: This balanced strategy targets moderate monthly gains (~2.5%) by reducing leverage and concentration while adding promising new names. It aims for risk-first growth, accepting slightly higher potential drawdowns than the conservative plan for better upside.

plan: Add to leveraged ETFs (SOXL to 6%, SPAL to 6%) for amplified gains.
Trim SPY to 25% to reduce concentration and free up capital.
Buy Netflix (NFLX) at 6% and ASML at 5% for high-growth potential.

aggressive.read: This aggressive strategy targets higher monthly gains (~4%) by increasing leverage and concentrating on high-scoring setups, including leveraged ETFs. It carries significantly higher risk of large drawdowns due to leverage and daily rebalancing of leveraged ETFs, requiring strict stop discipline.

plan: Sell all leveraged ETFs (SOXL, SPAL) to zero.
Trim SPY to 20% to reduce concentration and increase cash.
Significantly increase QQQI to 30% for enhanced income generation.
Trim CRWD to 5% to reduce exposure to high-beta single names.
Buy Microsoft (MSFT) at 10% as a stable, income-producing tech addition.
This plan prioritizes steady monthly distributions and capital preservation over growth.
income.read: This income-focused strategy aims for modest monthly distributions (~1%) by prioritizing income-generating assets and broad market exposure, while cutting high-risk single names and leverage. The primary risk is that distributions are variable and NAV can still decline in market downturns, though drawdowns are expected to be lower.
